Although `key` may be coerced to a model attribute for known column names, when `key` is NOT a known model attribute (the `elif json_column` branch at line 291 is taken), it remains a raw string from user input. `value` at this branch is also user-controlled (it is only checked for wildcards before reaching line 299). Neither `key` nor `value` are validated against any whitelist before being string-formatted into the Oracle `json_exists` SQL expression, making both susceptible to SQL injection. findings.suggested_fix:
Replace the unsafe string interpolation with a parameterised query using SQLAlchemy's `bindparams`. For example:

```python
expression = text("json_exists(meta, '$?(@.:key == :value)')").bindparams(key=key, value=str(value))
```
or, since Oracle's `json_exists` path expression syntax may not support bind parameters for key names, validate `key` strictly against the allowed model attribute names (whitelist) before use, and bind `value` as a parameter. At a minimum, `value` must never be string-interpolated; use bound parameters. For `key`, validate it is a known safe identifier (alphanumeric/underscore only) before interpolation.
findings.semgrep_message: SQLAlchemy text()/exec_driver_sql() with dynamic content may allow SQL injection if user input is interpolated. Verify that only bound parameters are used.

findings.explanation: In the PR, both `list_dids` (line 77) and `list_dids_extended` (line 109) contain a copy-paste bug where the `scope` filter key is internalized but mistakenly written to `or_group['account']` instead of `or_group['scope']`. The base code correctly wrote `filters['scope'] = InternalScope(filters['scope'], vo=vo)`. Because of this bug, when a caller supplies a `scope` filter, the VO-scoped `InternalScope` value (which carries the VO namespace prefix enforcing tenant isolation) is placed in the wrong key (`account`), and the original user-controlled external string in `or_group['scope']` is passed unchanged to the core `list_dids` / `list_dids_extended` layer. The core layer uses this raw, un-internalized scope value in database queries (via `FilterEngine`), which means the VO prefix is not applied, potentially allowing a user from one VO to query DIDs belonging to another VO's scope — a cross-VO authorization bypass.
findings.suggested_fix: Change `or_group['account'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` to `or_group['scope'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` in both `list_dids` (line 77) and `list_dids_extended` (line 109) so that the VO-namespaced InternalScope value is stored in the correct `scope` key and is properly enforced by the core query layer.

findings.explanation: The `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` method (introduced/moved in this PR) resolves a user-supplied filter key string directly to any attribute of the SQLAlchemy model class via `hasattr`/`getattr` with no allowlist check. A caller such as `list_dids` passes `model_class=models.DataIdentifier`, so any column name that exists on that model — including sensitive internal columns like `account`, `availability`, `suppressed`, `obsolete`, `monotonic`, `is_open`, etc. — can be used as a filter criterion by an unauthenticated or unprivileged user. The `manages_key`/`has_key` method in `did_column_meta.py` (lines 286-298) maintains an explicit exclusion list of sensitive columns that should not be exposed, but `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` completely bypasses that exclusion list: it grants access to any attribute `hasattr(model_class, word)` returns true for, which includes all the excluded columns. This allows users to probe or filter DIDs by columns that the project explicitly decided to hide (e.g., `suppressed`, `account`, `obsolete`).

findings.suggested_fix: Use Oracle's native bind-parameter syntax within the JSON_EXISTS expression, or use SQLAlchemy's bindparams mechanism so that both `key` and `value` are never interpolated as raw strings. For the key (column/attribute name), validate it against a strict allowlist of known JSON metadata keys before embedding it in the SQL text. For the value, use a bound parameter: e.g., `text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@." + validated_key + " == :val)')").bindparams(val=value)`.

findings.explanation: At line 299, a new code path introduced by this PR constructs a raw SQLAlchemy `text()` expression by directly interpolating user-controlled `key` and `value` into an Oracle JSON_EXISTS predicate string without any sanitisation or parameterisation. The `key` variable at this point is a plain Python `str` (it failed coercion to a model attribute because `strict_coerce=False` was used), meaning it comes directly from user-supplied filter input. The `value` variable, while passed through `_try_typecast_string`, remains a `str` here (the wildcard check above ensures it contains no `*`/`%`, but does not prevent SQL metacharacters). An attacker can craft a `key` or `value` containing Oracle SQL syntax to break out of the JSON_EXISTS predicate and inject arbitrary SQL. This code path did not exist before this PR; the old `create_sqla_query` had no `json_column` parameter and no `text()` call.
findings.suggested_fix: Never interpolate `key` or `value` directly into a `text()` SQL string. For the Oracle JSON_EXISTS case, use a bound parameter for `value` (e.g. via SQLAlchemy's `bindparam`) and validate/allowlist `key` against the known set of JSON metadata keys before constructing the expression. Example: validate `key` against an explicit allowlist of permitted metadata attribute names, and pass `value` as a bound parameter using SQLAlchemy's `func.json_exists` or a parameterised `text()` with `:val` placeholder.

findings.suggested_fix: Do not use string interpolation to build the Oracle JSON path expression. Instead, validate `key` against a strict allowlist of known JSON metadata keys before use, and use a bound parameter for `value`. For example: verify `key` matches `^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$` (or check it against a pre-approved set), then pass `value` as a bound parameter using SQLAlchemy's `bindparam` rather than embedding it directly in the `text()` string. If Oracle's `json_exists` does not support bind parameters in the path, cast and escape both `key` and `value` through a dedicated sanitiser that rejects any character outside the expected set.

findings.explanation: In the PR's updated filter_engine.py, when the database dialect is Oracle and the filter key has not been coerced to a model attribute (i.e. it is a JSON metadata key supplied by the caller), both `key` and `value` are interpolated directly into a raw SQL string via `.format()` and passed to SQLAlchemy's `text()`. The `key` comes from user-supplied filter dict keys (e.g. `{'mykey.gte': 'myvalue'}`) and `value` is the corresponding user-supplied filter value. Neither is sanitised, escaped, or bound as a parameter before being embedded in the SQL string. An attacker controlling filter key or value names can inject arbitrary Oracle SQL. This code path did not exist in the base snapshot — it was introduced by this PR.

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3

Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |

So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server.     rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
